Title: Local Reflexivity and Exactness for Reduced $C^*$-Algebras of Wreath Products
Authors: Pingchuan Dong, Zhe Dong
Date: Mon Oct 26 01:32:16 2026

We prove that, for every countable non-exact discrete group $H$ and every nontrivial countable discrete group $K$, the reduced group $C^*$-algebra $C_r^*(K\wr H)$ is not locally reflexive. These provide the first known examples of non-locally reflexive reduced group $C^*$-algebras, settling a longstanding existence question. Moreover, for every nontrivial countable exact discrete group $K$, we establish that local reflexivity of $C_r^*(K\wr H)$ is equivalent to exactness of $H$, and hence to exactness of $C_r^*(K\wr H)$. This gives a partial affirmative answer to Kirchberg's question of whether local reflexivity implies exactness for $C^*$-algebras. As applications, we construct finitely generated groups with the Haagerup property, as well as finitely generated residually finite groups, whose reduced group $C^*$-algebras are not locally reflexive. In particular, neither the Haagerup property nor coarse embeddability into Hilbert space guarantees local reflexivity of the associated reduced group $C^*$-algebra.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We address a structural gap in the quantitative theory of operator approximation by investigating how subspace approximation schemes interact with local reflexivity. Recent literature establishing the duality of scheme-relative approximation numbers, $a_n(T,Q) = a_n(T^{**}, Q^{\perp\perp})$, has relied on imposing an Extended Local Reflexivity Property (ELRP) as an independent axiom. In this note, we establish a dichotomy. For infinite-dimensional admissible schemes, we prove they naturally generate complete nests, perfectly satisfying the topological hypotheses of the Oja-Veidenberg Nest Principle of Local Reflexivity. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Basic metric notions

Let X = ( X , d ) be a metric space. For any x ∈ X and r > 0 , we use B ( x , r ) to denote the closed ball in X with center x and radius r . Given two subsets A , B ⊂ X , we write

d ( A , B ) = inf { d ( a , b ) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B }

to denote the infimal distance between A and B . To ease notation, we write d ( x , B ) for d ( { x } , B ) . We use

N r ( B ) = { x ∈ X : d ( x , B ) < r }

to denote the open r -neighborhood of B in X . A covering of X is, by definition, a collection ( B i ) i ∈ I of subsets of X such that ⋃ i ∈ I B i = X . For all coverings constructed in this article, we tacitly assume that they consist only of non-empty subsets. This does not cause any problems because whenever X is non-empty and the empty set is removed from a covering of X , the resulting collection is still a covering.

### 2.2 Pointwise Lipschitz constants

For any map f : X → Y between metric spaces, we denote by

Lip f ( x ) = limsup x ′ → x d ( f ( x ) , f ( x ′ ) ) d ( x , x ′ )

Recall that X is c -quasiconvex if any two points in X can be joined by a continuous path of length at most c times their distance.

## 7 Lipschitz n -connectedness

In practice, it is often necessary to extend Lipschitz maps, which do not have S n − 1 ⊂ R n as domain space but the boundary ∂ K of a convex body K ⊂ R n . For example, in view of Definition 6.1, it seems useful to know how to extend maps from the simplicial boundary of a simplex to the whole simplex. In the following, we investigate property LC ( n , λ ) not only for S n but also for other domain spaces.

## Definition 7.1

Let K ⊂ R n be a convex body, i.e., K is a compact convex set with non-empty interior. A metric space Y is said to satisfy condition LC ( K , λ ) if every L -Lipschitz map f : ∂ K → Y admits a λ L -Lipschitz extension F : K → Y .

It is easy to check that LC ( K , λ ) is translation and scale invariant, i.e., LC ( K , λ ) implies LC ( v + s K , λ ) for any v ∈ R n and s > 0 . Moreover, it also clearly holds that Y satisfies LC ( n , λ ) if and only if it satisfies LC ( B m , λ ) for every m = 1 , … , n + 1 . Since each convex body K ⊂ R n is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to B n via a boundary preserving map, it follows that LC ( K , λ ) and LC ( B n , λ ) differ only up to a multiplicative constant. The following lemma makes this more precise.

Introduced in the early 1990s by Kirchberg and Wassermann, the concept of exactness captures a fundamental approximation property related to how a C*-algebra interacts with short exact sequences under minimal tensor products. ... This is sometimes called the "local reflexivity" or "Ozawa's condition."
More precisely, for every short exact sequence of C*-algebras

0 → I → B → B/I → 0

the induced sequence

0 → A ⊗min I → A ⊗min B → A ⊗min (B/I) → 0

is also exact. Equivalently, the minimal tensor product of A with any quotient map B → B/I remains a quotient map, so that A ⊗min (B/I) is isomorphic to the quotient (A ⊗min B) / (A ⊗min I).

This definition can be stated more abstractly: A is exact if and only if the functor A ⊗min (−) from the category of C*-algebras to itself is exact in the categorical sense, preserving kernels and cokernels of morphisms.

### Alternative Characterizations

One of the remarkable features of exact C*-algebras is the abundance of equivalent characterizations. Kirchberg and Wassermann proved that the following conditions are equivalent for a separable C*-algebra A:

  1. A is exact (as defined above).
  2. A can be embedded into the Cuntz algebra O₂ (or any other sufficiently large purely infinite simple C*-algebra).
  3. A admits an amenable action on a compact space.
  4. A is isomorphic to a subalgebra of a nuclear C*-algebra.
  5. For any finite subset F ⊆ A and any ε > 0, there exist a finite-dimensional C*-algebra D and completely positive maps φ : A → D and ψ : D → A such that ||ψ(φ(a)) − a|| < ε for all a ∈ F. This is sometimes called the "local reflexivity" or "Ozawa's condition."

The equivalence of exactness with embeddability into nuclear C*-algebras is particularly illuminating: it shows that exact C*-algebras are precisely those that can be viewed as subalgebras of well-behaved algebras.

Ozawa provided yet another characterization in terms of the notion of amenability for operator algebras, showing that a C*-algebra is exact if and only if it admits a hyperlinear representation with certain approximation properties.

TRACIALLY COMPLETE C∗-ALGEBRAS

JOS´

E R. CARRI ´

ON, JORGE CASTILLEJOS, SAMUEL EVINGTON, JAMES GABE,

CHRISTOPHER SCHAFHAUSER, AARON TIKUISIS, AND STUART WHITE

Abstract. We introduce a new class of operator algebras – tracially

complete C∗-algebras – as a vehicle for transferring ideas and results

between C∗-algebras and their tracial von Neumann algebra comple-

tions. We obtain structure and classiﬁcation results for amenable tra-

cially complete C∗-algebras satisfying an appropriate version of Murray

and von Neumann’s property Γ for II 1 factors. In a precise sense, these

results ﬁt between Connes’ celebrated theorems for injective II 1 factors

and the unital classiﬁcation theorem for separable simple nuclear C∗-

algebras. The theory also underpins arguments for the known parts of

the Toms–Winter conjecture.
